item.title: Dengue takes deadlier turn
item.description:
Bangladesh’s dengue outbreak has taken a sharply deadlier turn in September, with 74 people dying in just 16 days, already 72% more than the 43 deaths recorded throughout August, as hospital admissions surged to their highest daily level of the year.
The pace of deaths has more than tripled.
September has so far claimed an average of 4.6 lives a day, compared with about 1.4 in August, according to a Dhaka Tribune analysis of Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) data.
Seven more people died and 1,753 were hospitalised in the 24 hours to Wednesday morning, taking this year’s toll to 171 deaths and 56,916 hospital admissions.
The latest caseload is the highest recorded in a single day this year, underscoring how rapidly the outbreak has intensified since the monsoon.
The deterioration is not confined to deaths.
Bangladesh recorded 9,206 hospitalizations in July before cases more than doubled to 20,536 in August.
September is now accumulating patients at an even faster pace, with more than 1,000 admissions being reported almost every day.
Of Wednesday’s 1,753 admissions, 744 were in Dhaka and surrounding areas, while Khulna recorded 349, Barisal 186, Chittagong 177, Rajshahi 153, Mymensingh 83, Rangpur 53 and Sylhet nine.
The seven latest deaths, however, all occurred outside Dhaka -- three in Khulna and one each in Chittagong, Mymensingh, Rajshahi and Rangpur -- highlighting the outbreak’s widening geographical reach.
Dhaka nevertheless accounts for the largest share of fatalities this year, with 80 deaths, followed by Khulna with 32, Mymensingh 18, Chittagong 16, Barisal 13, Rajshahi eight, Rangpur three and Sylhet one.
Public health experts warned that hospital figures alone do not necessarily reflect where transmission is highest because critically ill patients from districts are often referred to Dhaka.
Renowned entomologist Professor Kabirul Bashar of Jahangirnagar University, said: “Dengue is no longer concentrated in Dhaka. Cases are rising in several districts, including Khulna, Patuakhali, Bagerhat, Chapainawabganj, Bandarban, Pirojpur, Chittagong, Munshiganj and Narayanganj.”
“Dhaka hospitals show higher numbers partly because patients from across the country come to the capital for advanced treatment. Controlling dengue requires effective vector management and community participation, not merely insecticide use.”
Former DGHS disease control director Professor Be-Nazir Ahmed said: “Fogging alone cannot control dengue. The most effective measure is to identify and destroy Aedes mosquito breeding sites. At the same time, rapid diagnosis and timely treatment are crucial to preventing severe illness and deaths.”
The trajectory has worsened sharply since July, and experts fear infections and deaths could continue rising through November without stronger preventive measures.
With September only halfway through, its death toll has already far surpassed August’s, while the latest record hospital admissions suggest the outbreak has yet to peak.

item.title: Are brighter nights extending Aedes biting hours?
item.description:
As Bangladesh’s cities grow brighter after sunset, researchers are confronting an unsettling change in the behaviour of the mosquito responsible for spreading dengue: Aedes is no longer necessarily calling it a day when darkness falls.
Aedes mosquitoes, traditionally considered predominantly daytime biters, are increasingly being observed active after sunset in Bangladesh.
Laboratory and field research abroad has also found that artificial light at night can increase or prolong mosquito activity.
The findings raise a question with potentially important implications for Bangladesh’s dengue control strategy: could increasingly illuminated urban nights be extending the hours in which people are exposed to Aedes bites?
There is no direct evidence yet that Dhaka’s LED streetlights or other artificial lighting are increasing dengue transmission.
Researchers caution that establishing such a link would require Bangladesh-specific studies comparing mosquito behaviour under different lighting conditions.
But the question has assumed greater urgency as Bangladesh faces another severe dengue season, with transmission spreading well beyond Dhaka.
Professor Kabirul Bashar, a zoologist at Jahangirnagar University who has extensively studied Aedes mosquitoes, said their nighttime activity can no longer be ignored.
“The density of Aedes mosquitoes is slightly lower at night. However, Aedes mosquitoes still bite during nighttime,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
“Previously, these mosquitoes used to bite only during the day, specifically in the morning and afternoon.”
Research conducted by Bashar and colleagues between 2021 and 2023 collected 134,904 mosquitoes from Jahangirnagar University, Savar, Chittagong and Cox’s Bazar.
Monitoring between 4pm and 9pm found Aedes mosquitoes remaining active into the evening, including around 9pm.
The study establishes that Aedes can remain active after sunset in Bangladesh, but it did not compare areas according to artificial-light exposure.
It therefore cannot establish whether brighter nights are responsible.
What is clear is that Dhaka’s nighttime environment has changed dramatically.
A 2026 study published in Environmental Sciences Europe, using VIIRS satellite observations from 2014 to 2023, documented a substantial expansion of artificial nighttime illumination in Dhaka, with researchers estimating an annual increase of 7.2%.
Some of the brightest concentrations were around the airport, Gulshan, Banani, Dhanmondi, Motijheel and Tejgaon.
Across Dhaka and other major cities, older streetlights have increasingly given way to brighter white LED systems, while commercial areas, buildings and public spaces remain illuminated for longer.
The satellite findings establish the expansion of nighttime light, not a connection with dengue.
International research, however, offers a possible biological mechanism.
A 2020 laboratory experiment found 82% of female Aedes aegypti fed during daytime under normal experimental conditions, compared with 29% at night.
After a 30-minute exposure to white light, nighttime feeding increased to 59%.
A 2025 US field study of Aedes albopictus at 58 locations similarly found greater nighttime activity at sites experiencing higher artificial-light pollution, particularly following very hot days.
Neither finding can be directly extrapolated to Bangladesh because mosquito species, climate and real-world lighting conditions differ.
Professor Humayun Reza Khan of Dhaka University’s Zoology Department said those limitations make local research essential.
“Artificial light at night can affect animal behaviour, but the nature and extent of that effect can vary from one species to another,” he said.
“We cannot say exactly how light pollution is affecting a particular animal or mosquito species without conducting specific research.”
For Bangladesh, that would mean comparing Aedes activity in otherwise similar neighbourhoods with different levels and types of illumination, while measuring brightness, wavelength, colour temperature, duration and nighttime temperatures.
Until such research is conducted, brighter streets cannot be blamed for Bangladesh’s dengue surge.
But as cities remain awake, and illuminated, for longer, scientists say an old assumption underlying dengue prevention may warrant reconsideration: that the mosquito biting people during the day rests when night falls.

item.title: In school, but failing to learn
item.description:
Bangladesh has succeeded in getting most children into classrooms, but a nationwide survey has exposed a deeper crisis: millions are progressing through school without mastering the basic reading and mathematics skills on which the rest of their education depends.
More than six in 10 children aged seven to 14, 60.8%, cannot demonstrate foundational mathematical skills, while 49.8% fail to meet the minimum standard for reading and understanding a simple, age-appropriate story, according to the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025.
The findings from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS)-Unicef survey expose a stark disconnect between school participation and actual learning.
Among children in Grades 2 and 3, only 28.2% demonstrated foundational reading skills, while just 20.8% could perform basic mathematical tasks such as recognizing and comparing numbers, addition and identifying patterns.
Even by Grade 5, only 62% demonstrated foundational reading skills.
The survey also reveals that being able to read words does not necessarily mean children understand them.
While 61.6% of seven- to 14-year-olds could correctly read at least 90% of the words in a story, only 50.2% could also answer the required comprehension questions.
Recent National Student Assessment findings reinforce the concern: 91% of Grade 5 students were classified at the “novice” level in mathematics and 65% in Bangla.
Learning deficiencies are compounded by a sharp decline in attendance as children grow older.
Net attendance falls from 85.1% at primary level to 60.1% at lower secondary and 50.8% at upper secondary. By upper-secondary age, 33.9% of children are out of school.
Only 43.9% complete upper secondary education, compared with 83.7% completing primary.
Economic inequality compounds the problem.
Only 33.6% of children from the poorest fifth of households demonstrate foundational reading skills, compared with 67.4% from the richest fifth.
At upper-secondary level, just 21% of children from the poorest households complete their education, against 69.3% among the richest.
Urban children also outperform their rural counterparts in foundational reading, 55.6% to 48%.
The weaknesses begin before children enter primary school.
Only 16.6% of children aged 36–59 months participate in early childhood education, while just 8.5% of seven- to 14-year-olds have at least three books at home besides textbooks.
Girls outperform boys in foundational reading, with 54.5% meeting the standard compared with 45.6% of boys.
Delayed entry also remains widespread: 38.4% of children do not begin Grade 1 at the appropriate age.
Educationist Professor Anu Muhammad said inadequate classroom teaching, dependence on coaching and private tuition, guidebooks and memorization were preventing children from developing genuine understanding.
“As a result, children are failing to properly master two of the most fundamental areas of early learning, language and mathematics,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
He also pointed to inadequate public investment, teacher shortages, infrastructure and curriculum weaknesses.
The MICS findings are based on 62,980 households and assessments of 34,990 children aged seven to 14 across all 64 districts.
Taken together, the numbers point to a challenge beyond enrolment: Bangladesh is keeping many children in school without ensuring that they learn the fundamentals needed to progress through it.

item.title: Jurain: An island of suffering in the capital
item.description:
Just west of Jurain Railgate, the trappings of the capital begin to disappear.
Beneath and around the elevated expressway connecting Mayor Hanif Flyover towards Padma Bridge lies a densely populated neighbourhood where residents say a decade of neglect has left them battling broken roads, stagnant sewage-mixed water, unreliable gas and electricity, unsafe water supplies and an escalating mosquito menace.
Locals now describe Jurain as an “island of suffering” inside Dhaka -- and, frustrated by years of complaints and promises, say they are preparing a larger movement demanding basic civic services.
The contrast is stark.
Jurain is part of Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC), yet residents say some roads have remained virtually impassable for years and even modest rainfall can leave neighbourhoods inundated for weeks.
From Jurain Junction towards Mishtir Mor, one road south of the Bikrampur Complex has remained impassable for years, according to residents. When rain comes, accumulated water spreads into surrounding areas.
“Then it seems that we are living in hell even though we are residents of the capital,” resident Bulbul Ahmed said, describing floodwater entering homes.
Farhana Islam voiced the same frustration.
“Are we residents of the capital?” she asked.
“Only waterlogging, no gas, no electricity, mosquitoes; all in all it seems as if we people of Jurain are from another planet.”
She alleged politicians arrive with promises during elections but disappear afterwards.
Residents said Jurain Railgate, Commissioner Road and areas around Vikrampur Plaza can go under waist-deep water during rain.
They blame clogged drains and a dysfunctional drainage network.
The stagnant water can remain for weeks, producing a foul smell and flooding ground-floor homes and shops.
Some roads, including Madrasa Road and Medical Road, remain under dark, foul-smelling water for extended periods, residents alleged.
Road conditions compound the danger.
Broken surfaces and large potholes disappear beneath accumulated water, causing rickshaws and autorickshaws to overturn, according to observations in the area.
Even clean water has become a concern.
Residents alleged that water supplied in parts of Jurain is dirty and foul-smelling, with leakage allowing drain water to contaminate pipelines.
They said repeated protests, including human chains demanding safe water, have failed to bring lasting improvement.
Gas shortages add another layer of hardship.
Residents said supply can disappear in the morning and return only late at night, forcing households to rely on LPG cylinders or kerosene despite continuing to pay gas bills.
Persistent stagnant water and poor waste management have also heightened concern over dengue.
A pre-monsoon Aedes survey identified 27 DSCC wards as being at “extreme risk”, including Ward 53 in Jurain.
Aedes density exceeded the established threshold in 63 of DSCC’s 75 wards.
DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam said the government was making every effort to contain dengue and pointed to a three-month special campaign aimed at mosquito control and public awareness.
But residents say their patience is running out.
On September 4, residents of Shyampur-Kadamtali staged a protest and torch procession at the railgate under the slogan “No Gas, No Bill”, and organisers say preparations are underway for a broader movement.
“We’ve worn out the soles of our shoes going around pleading with officials,” local campaigner Mizanur Rahman said, alleging residents had spent nearly a decade seeking solutions.
Another resident, Ashraf Hossain, said people pay city corporation taxes but still lack basic amenities and are preparing to take to the streets until their demands are addressed.
Asked about the complaints, Salam said no one had approached DSCC with them.
On drainage, however, he acknowledged that the problem extended beyond Jurain.
“It is not just Jurain; the drainage systems in many parts of Dhaka are in poor condition,” he said. “Initiatives have been taken to address these issues, but it will take time.”

item.title: Jamaat questions EC’s ability to ensure fair local polls
item.description:
Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Secretary General Mia Golam Parwar has questioned whether free and fair local government elections can be held under the current Election Commission (EC).
Speaking at a press conference at the party’s central office on Wednesday, he alleged that the EC was operating according to the government’s instructions and could not function independently.
Parwar also alleged that the government was pushing opposition parties toward boycotting elections.
He further claimed that the government had appointed ruling party members as administrators in various places, making it difficult to ensure a level playing field and hold a neutral election.
At the briefing, Parwar presented eight demands concerning the local government elections.
He demanded adequate time and opportunities for all candidates, a safe environment and a level playing field, and warned that no excuse for delaying the election would be accepted.
The Jamaat leader said the administration and law enforcement agencies must not be used for any political interest. He also called on the government to ensure that the EC could perform its duties independently.
Parwar said Jamaat-e-Islami had raised several demands during meetings with the EC over the local government elections.
The demands included declaring administrators ineligible to contest the elections and allowing MPO-listed teachers and officials to participate.
Meanwhile, the EC has said preparations are underway to hold the local government elections.
According to a recent statement by the EC secretary, a schedule for holding the elections in several phases had been discussed initially.
Also present at the briefing were Jamaat Assistant Secretary General and parliamentary party whip Rafiqul Islam Khan, Dr Hamidur Rahman Azad and Ahsanul Mahboob Zubair, among others.

item.title: Awami League procession: Gulshan DC withdrawn after OC
item.description:
The deputy commissioner (DC) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Gulshan Division, M Tanvir Ahmed, has been withdrawn from his post and attached to DMP headquarters, hours after the officer-in-charge (OC) of Gulshan Model Police Station was removed, five days after a procession by the activity-banned Awami League and its affiliated organizations in the capital’s Gulshan area.
DMP Commissioner Mosleh Uddin Ahmed signed an office order on Wednesday, attaching Tanvir Ahmed to DMP headquarters until further orders.
The order instructed him to hand over charge to the next senior officer and report to DMP headquarters. It cited administrative reasons for the decision.
Earlier on Wednesday, Gulshan Model Police Station OC Md Daud Hossain was also withdrawn and attached to the Central Reserve Office under the DMP headquarters and Administration Division.
The two officers were withdrawn five days after leaders and activists of the banned Awami League and its affiliated organizations brought out a procession on Road 3 near KFC in Gulshan on Friday.
Police moved to disperse the procession, during which two crude bombs were detonated, according to police. Police subsequently fired two rounds of rubber bullets to bring the situation under control. Two people were arrested at the scene and five unexploded crude bombs were recovered, police said.
A case was later filed at Gulshan Police Station under the Anti-Terrorism Act. Police had arrested 83 people in connection with the case by September 14, according to reports.
The DMP has cited administrative reasons for the withdrawal of both officers and has not publicly specified any allegation against them or directly linked the orders to the procession.
Speaking at an event at the secretariat on Tuesday, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said intelligence agencies had information about the planned procession in Gulshan.
He said police may not have anticipated that people who had gathered in the area for Friday prayers would later engage in such activities.
Referring to the incident, the home minister said some people had gathered in the area around 11am on the pretext of offering Friday prayers and that action was subsequently taken against them.

item.title: Bobby Hajjaj: Govt plans new policy to improve primary school safety
item.description:
The government is planning to introduce a new policy to ensure the safety of infrastructure and facilities at around 150,000 primary schools across the country, State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj said on Wednesday.
He made the remarks while addressing the Safeguarding Leadership Summit 2026, jointly organized by Haileybury Bhaluka and Cambridge University Press and Assessment at the Sky Ballroom of Le Méridien Dhaka.
Hajjaj said the proposed policy would cover various issues related to students’ safety and wellbeing, including dengue prevention, infrastructure renovation, access to safe drinking water and proper WASH (water, sanitation and hygiene) facilities.
He also said life-saving skills would be incorporated into the primary curriculum through monthly themes.
“Going forward, life-saving skills such as fire safety, traffic rules and water hazards will be incorporated into the curriculum as monthly themes. Students will not only learn these things from books but also gain practical experience by visiting places such as fire stations,” he said.
The state minister said around 800,000 to one million teachers would need training to effectively implement the initiatives.
He called on Cambridge and other international organizations to work with the government as partners beyond commercial interests.
He also stressed the role of parent-teacher associations and local communities in ensuring children’s safety.
The summit, themed “Stronger Together, Safer Tomorrow – Keeping Children Safe in Bangladesh,” brought together school leaders, teachers, educators, policymakers and safeguarding professionals to discuss child protection and safer learning environments.
Speaking at the event, Simon O’Grady, founding headmaster of Haileybury Bhaluka, said safeguarding should be treated as part of an institution’s culture rather than merely a checklist or policy.
“Safeguarding is not a checklist or a policy on paper, it is an institutional culture. A good school leader must be visible, curious, courageous and consistent,” he said.
He added that safety was a prerequisite for creativity and that children should be able to speak about their concerns without fear.
“A child feels safe when they can speak without fear and have the courage to report an incident to the authorities,” O’Grady said.
Sarwat Reza, country lead at Cambridge University Press & Assessment, also attended the summit, along with education leaders and safeguarding experts from different parts of the country.
Speakers also stressed that child safeguarding cannot be limited to a single policy or designated individual. They called for stronger leadership, accountability, professional training and greater involvement of the wider school community to create safer and more inclusive learning environments.

item.title: Court orders seizure, freezing of Abul Barakat’s assets
item.description:
A Dhaka court has ordered the seizure and freezing of movable and immovable assets belonging to former Janata Bank PLC chairman Dr Abul Barkat over allegations of illegally sanctioning loans to various companies and acquiring assets disproportionate to his known sources of income.
Dhaka Metropolitan Senior Special Judge Shahjahan Kabir passed the order on Wednesday following an application filed by Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) investigating officer and Assistant Director Mohammad Shahjahan Miraj.
The assets include an investment of Tk2.5 lakh in the Dhaka University Teachers’ Housing Project and two flats in Mohammadpur and Dhanmondi. A vehicle valued at Tk29 lakh and funds held in bank accounts in his name have also been frozen.
According to court documents, the ACC is conducting an inquiry into allegations that Barkat illegally provided loans to various institutions and acquired assets inconsistent with his known sources of income.
The application said the inquiry had so far uncovered immovable assets worth Tk49.61 lakh and movable assets worth Tk3.50 crore and $10,250 in his name.
It further said information obtained from various sources indicated that Barkat was attempting to sell or transfer assets linked to the allegations.
The ACC argued that any transfer, conversion or sale of the allegedly illegal assets before the inquiry is concluded could cause significant financial loss to the state.
It therefore sought the immediate seizure and freezing of the assets under Section 14 of the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012 and Rule 18 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Rules 2007.
The application also said freezing the assets was necessary to prevent their transfer or disposal before the allegations are resolved.
Barkat was arrested from his Dhanmondi residence on July 10, 2025, in an ACC case. After securing bail in that case, he was shown arrested in a case over the killing of businessman Wadud in connection with the July uprising.
He was later granted bail in that case and released from jail on June 20.

item.title: Palestinians are the real victims, Thunberg tells Ed Sheeran
item.description:
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg and other activists have called out British superstar Ed Sheeran after rapper Macklemore was dropped from his tour for making pro-Palestinian comments while performing.
Sheeran has denied being behind the decision to remove Macklemore, saying his tour’s promoter was responsible, but several supporting acts have announced they were quitting the tour.
“Ed, there is only one victim here: the Palestinian people,” Thunberg, together with activist group Humanti Project, said in post to Instagram late on Tuesday.
According to a post by Sheeran, where he stressed the decision was the promoters, venues on the tour “communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting.”
Finneas -- a performer also famous for work with his superstar sister Billie Eilish -- Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, and Lukas Graham of Denmark have all posted they were quitting Sheeran’s “Loop Tour.”
“This is a clear and undeniable sign that the global consciousness has shifted. The normalization of an apartheid state, and the attempts to sanitize or justify its actions, will no longer be tolerated,” the post shared by Thunberg said.
While opening for Sheeran earlier this month at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, Macklemore shouted “Free Palestine!” and told Palestinians they were “not forgotten.”
In his post Tuesday, Sheeran touched on his decision not to comment publicly about political subjects, notably the war in Gaza.
“I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t care,” he said.
Macklemore, known for hits including “Thrift Shop” and “Can’t Hold Us,” has long vocally supported Palestinians.
In 2024 he released “Hind’s Hall,” which pays tribute to Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl whose death sparked a wave of international outrage.

item.title: Forming a parliamentary caucus for change: A national push for disability rights
item.description:
A cross-party Parliamentary Caucus on Disability Rights is set to be formed with lawmakers from four political parties, creating a dedicated platform in the 13 th National Parliament to push disability-inclusive legislation and budgets, scrutinise government commitments and strengthen the political representation of persons with disabilities.
State Minister for Health and Family Welfare Dr MA Muhit MP has unanimously been chosen as chairman of the proposed caucus, while BNP Standing Committee member and MP Selima Rahman and Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Women’s Wing Secretary Nurunnisa Siddiqua MP will serve as deputy chairs.
The commitments came at a High-Level Consultation on the Formation of a Parliamentary Caucus on Disability Rights, jointly organised by Sightsavers’ Equal Bangladesh Campaign, Democracy International and the Blind Education and Rehabilitation Development Organization (BERDO) in Dhaka.
The proposed caucus would advocate for disability-inclusive legislation and adequate budget allocations, expedite and monitor implementation of existing laws, government commitments and election manifestos of political parties, and bring disability concerns into the work of ministries and parliamentary standing committees.
It would also establish regular engagement between lawmakers and persons with disabilities, Organisations of People with Disabilities (OPDs), civil society and development partners, giving those directly affected by disability-related barriers a stronger voice in policymaking.
Speakers highlighted persistent barriers in education, employment, healthcare, transport, social protection and public services, while also calling for accessible elections and digital services.
A keynote presentation by independent researcher Dr Nafeesur Rahman called for a shift from viewing persons with disabilities as recipients of charity to recognising them as rights-holders and part of human diversity.
He said the caucus should monitor implementation of disability laws and election manifestos declared by the political parties, and ensure disability inclusion is reflected in national budgets, surveys, policies, and legislation.
“Disability is not about inability, but the barriers society creates. Persons with disabilities need equal rights, access and opportunities, not charity or sympathy. The proposed parliamentary caucus can bring disability issues into every ministry and parliamentary standing committee. The caucus can act as a pressure group in the Parliament eliciting healthy debates amongst the parliamentarians to advance the rights of persons with disabilities.”
“Disability inclusion must begin at the family and grassroots levels. Allowances alone are not enough; persons with disabilities need education, skills and opportunities. We must change attitudes, properly implement existing laws and ensure the caucus brings their concerns to Parliament to build an inclusive, discrimination-free society.”
“Persons with disabilities are citizens entitled to full rights, dignity and opportunities. With proper education, skills and employment, they can become self-reliant and contribute to society. The government and society must remove discrimination and create an inclusive environment. I endorse the parliamentary caucus.”
“Parliamentary caucuses must be active and action-oriented, not exist in name only. The caucus should develop clear action plans consulting with disability rights organisations and ensure accountability, accessibility and protection from abuse, particularly for women with disabilities. Strong political commitment and coordinated action can make it an effective platform.”
“We must first change our mindset towards persons with disabilities. No child with a disability should be hidden or treated as a burden. Equal access to education, employment and vocational training, particularly in rural areas, requires sustained commitment and action. With proper opportunities, persons with disabilities can become economically independent and contribute equally to society.”
“Today’s discussion has changed my perspective on disability rights. I have seen the challenges persons with disabilities face, including helping someone regain a job after unfair dismissal. I strongly support the caucus and am committed to raising their concerns in Parliament.”
“Today’s discussion has been deeply moving. As an opposition MP, I assure you that we will raise our voices for the rights of persons with disabilities in Parliament and through our respective standing committees. Their struggles and determination strengthen our commitment to addressing the challenges they face.”
“Disability rights are not a matter of charity or sympathy but fundamental constitutional rights. ‘Nothing about us without us’ must guide our approach. Persons with disabilities deserve equal access to education, skills, employment and opportunities. I am committed to raising their voices through the parliamentary caucus and working for an inclusive society.”
“Persons with disabilities have been overlooked in efforts to build a discrimination-free Bangladesh. They are an integral part of society and deserve equal opportunities, not charity. Parliament must become their voice and ensure their rights to education, employment and participation.”
“Disability can occur at any stage of life. We must prioritise education, skills and employment so persons with disabilities can become financially independent, alongside social protection. Increasing disability allowances should also be considered, while qualified persons with disabilities must receive appropriate opportunities.”
“Disability inclusion must begin with families and communities. Girls with disabilities often face additional barriers and fewer opportunities. Every child with a disability must have access to appropriate education, while safe transport, social security and protection from sexual harassment require coordinated action by the state, society and families.”
“Disability allowances need to be increased, as persons with disabilities often face higher healthcare, mobility and living costs. Through the parliamentary caucus and relevant ministries, greater attention should be given to our financial needs and social protection.”
“Disability inclusion in political decision-making is about constitutional rights, dignity and equal citizenship, not charity. Bangladesh needs effective implementation of disability laws, disability-responsive budgeting, accountable policymaking and meaningful representation. The caucus can keep disability issues visible in Parliament and reflected in national policies and budgets.”
“Many persons with disabilities are of voting age, yet only a small number can effectively exercise their voting rights. Political parties and parliamentarians must pay greater attention. The caucus can ensure their voices and rights are reflected in political decision-making and make disability inclusion part of the democratic agenda.”
“Bangladesh has disability rights laws and committees, but they must function effectively. The caucus can bridge the gap between disability organisations and parliamentarians, strengthen political representation and ensure disability rights are reflected in policies, budgets and electoral processes.”
“A caucus on disability rights can make signification contribution in advancing our rights, and Bangladesh has the example of a functional caucus on disability rights in 2009. Based on that experience, the caucus will require a secretariat for which Sightsavers is the most suitable organisation. Regular meetings and sustained engagement will be essential to make the caucus effective and keep disability rights on the parliamentary agenda.”
“Employment remains a major challenge for persons with visual disabilities. The caucus should advocate for employment and ensure every law and bill considers disability rights. Inclusive education, accessible facilities, trained teachers and learning materials are also essential. With no direct representation in Parliament, the caucus should serve as their voice.”
“We must shift from treating persons with disabilities as objects of charity to recognising them as rights-holders and part of human diversity. This rights-based approach must begin in Parliament. The caucus should monitor disability laws and ensure disability inclusion in national budgets, surveys, policies and legislation.”
“Disability cannot be treated solely as the responsibility of the Ministry of Social Welfare. It must be incorporated into every ministry’s work and budget. Greater attention is also needed to disability-inclusive disaster preparedness and to ensuring persons with disabilities are included across public services and development programs.”
“Committees under the disability rights act are not functioning effectively. The caucus can bridge the gap between parliamentarians and persons with disabilities and advocate for political representation and accessible elections. Accessibility, including at polling centres, must be treated as a matter of dignity and rights.”
“‘Nothing about us without us.’ Persons with disabilities must participate in decisions affecting them. Accessibility goes beyond ramps and lifts to digital services. Many visually impaired people cannot independently use banking apps or government software because they are incompatible with screen readers or accessible CAPTCHA. Parliament must ensure accessible laws, policies and digital services.”
“The caucus is essential because persons with disabilities have very limited representation in Parliament and policymaking. It must ensure meaningful participation of women, men, young people and experienced persons with disabilities, while addressing barriers involving quotas, transportation and accessibility so they can participate equally in public life.”
“There are many persons with disabilities who are educated but unemployed though many posts are vacant in various ministries including in the Ministry of Social Welfare.”
“Political parties, the larger and smaller ones, are not willing to include us. I think we should have a political party of our own otherwise the government does not want to listen to us!”

item.title: Milestone School teacher killed in Banasree road crash
item.description:
A schoolteacher was killed after a bus crashed into a motorcycle she was riding pillion on in the capital’s Banasree area on Wednesday night.

The deceased was identified as Tasfiya Ahmed Tisha, 31, a teacher at Milestone School and daughter of Md Shafiuddin Ahmed of Meradia Noyapara in Khilgaon.

Tisha was riding a Pathao motorcycle when a bus of Ramjan Paribahan approaching from the opposite direction hit it near Farazy Hospital around 9:30 pm, according to her family.

Pedestrians and police personnel rescued her and rushed her to the emergency department of Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH), where physicians declared her dead.

Tisha’s brother Enam Ahmed said the family went to the hospital after receiving news of the accident. He said they were informed that police detained the bus driver and seized the vehicle.

DMCH police camp in-charge Inspector Habibur Rahman said the body has been kept at the hospital morgue for autopsy.

Despite the reduction of duties and taxes on more than 50 essential items—including agricultural products, solar equipment, computers, electrical goods, and spices—in the current FY27 budget, the benefits are not reaching the market.
Prices of most items remain unchanged, while some have unexpectedly increased.
Consequently, the tax exemptions are failing to translate into lower prices for consumers at the retail level.
However, traders justify the price hikes citing various factors, including the conflict in the Middle East, rising fuel costs, domestic energy shortages, floods, and heavy rainfall.
Experts emphasize that merely reducing or waiving taxes is insufficient; it is crucial to analyze and monitor whether the benefits actually reach the consumer level.
The new government's first budget was presented on June 11. It reduced taxes on 63 essential commodities.
Duty was completely withdrawn on all imported spices. Source tax on the import and supply stages of around 60 basic agricultural and consumer items—including rice, flour, wheat, pulses, potatoes, onions, garlic, ginger, salt, sugar, and edible oil—was lowered to 0.5%.
According to data from the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh (TCB) as of September 11, loose soybean oil prices rose by 11.40% year-on-year, while bottled soybean oil prices increased by 6% to 9%.
Prices of various spices increased by 10% to 16%, sugar by 2.27%, and standard-quality dates by 16.88%.
On September 2, the Ministry of Commerce approved a traders' proposal to increase the price of bottled soybean oil by Tk5 per liter. Previously priced at Tk199 per liter, bottled soybean oil now costs Tk204, following an initial proposal by traders to raise the price by Tk10.
In the retail market, coarse rice is selling at Tk52–55 per kg, BR-28 rice at Tk60, Miniket at Tk72, Nazirshail at Tk88, and Katari Nazir at Tk85 per kg.
However, Miniket prices vary depending on brand and quality. Wholesale traders also report price hikes, noting that a 50 kg sack of Miniket rice rose by about Tk50-60 over the past week.
Industry sources report that while general rice prices fluctuate, aromatic rice prices have surged significantly. Aromatic rice brands that sold for Tk160–200 per kg a month ago have now climbed to Tk170–215 per kg.
Other industries feel the pinch
The budget also granted tax benefits to laptops, desktop computers, servers, printers, and monitors.
Minimum tariff values were reduced across seven product categories, including lipsticks, skin creams, moisturizing lotions, and face washes.
Tax exemptions were also extended to medical equipment, electric vehicles, and solar products. Yet, positive market impacts remain largely unseen.
The country has been facing a severe energy crisis for several months. Reduced power generation has led to nationwide load-shedding, negatively impacting industries.
Consequently, many are turning to solar power as an alternative energy source.
However, despite duty and tax cuts, prices for solar products in Dhaka markets have not dropped; instead, increased demand has pushed prices higher in some cases.
A field visit to Nawabpur, Kaptan Bazar, Sundarban Square, and Gulistan Stadium markets revealed that a 550-watt solar panel sells for Tk13,500-19,500.
A 5-kW inverter costs between Tk48,000 and Tk77,000, while a 5.12 kWh lithium battery ranges from Tk98,000 to Tk130,000.
Purchasing these three core components alone costs between Tk160,000 and Tk225,000.
Furthermore, a 2,000 to 2,500-watt solar hybrid setup sells for Tk150,000 to Tk200,000.
Contrary to expectations of lower costs post-tax cuts, buyers are paying just as much or more.
Under the National Board of Revenue's (NBR) measures for the new fiscal year, import duty on lithium-ion batteries was reduced from 25% to zero, and solar panel duty was cut from 1% to zero.
Solar inverters were also granted complete duty exemption, along with conditional relief on steel and aluminum mounting structures, battery cells, and battery packs.
In the tech market, 8 GB DDR4 RAM sells for Tk6,000-8,000. Certain models of 16 GB DDR5 RAM, which cost roughly Tk12,000 to Tk16,000 in June, have climbed to nearly Tk28,000-33,000.
The price of a 512 GB SSD increased from around Tk5,000–7,000 in June to Tk9,000–Tk10,000 currently.
Entry-level 2 GB graphics cards range from Tk5,500 to Tk11,000.
However, industry sources note that computer monitor prices have decreased by about 20% due to tax cuts.
SM Nazer Hossain, vice president of the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB), stated that tax cuts have had no tangible impact on retail markets, where prices have not decreased by a single penny.
He urged the government to monitor whether tax concessions—worth thousands of crores of Taka—are reaching ordinary consumers or being siphoned off by intermediaries.

item.title: Who will compensate for the financial strain amid Dhaka’s gas crisis?
item.description:
For families in several parts of Dhaka, the gas crisis is no longer simply a cooking problem. Many households are paying monthly gas bills to the government authority despite receiving little or no gas, while also spending more on electricity, LPG, restaurant meals and other alternatives to cope with the shortage.
In Dhanmondi 7/A, residents said they had not received any gas for the past two months but had continued to pay their bills to Titas Gas.
In Lalbagh, housewife Faria Ahmed Borsha said her family had received virtually no gas for the past three to four months, although they continued to pay Titas Gas Tk1,080 every month.
This has become the norm in many parts of Dhaka, with households relying on alternative arrangements to meet their daily needs while continuing to pay for a gas service they are unable to use.
However, several Titas Gas officials told Dhaka Tribune that they do not have exact data on how many household consumers in Dhaka are not receiving gas.
Dhaka Tribune spoke to households affected by the shortage in Uttara, Pallabi, Mirpur, Mohammadpur, Kazipara, Shewrapara, Taltala, Dhanmondi, Lalmatia, Lalbagh, Shukrabad and Farmgate. Most said the shortage had disrupted cooking and forced them to spend more on alternatives while continuing to pay their monthly gas bills.
The acute gas crisis has caused suffering in many areas of Dhaka for the past two to three months, with residents facing additional expenses to cook food, heat water and meet other basic household needs.
This has raised a question among consumers: Who will compensate them for the additional financial burden when they are paying their monthly gas bills but receiving little or no gas?
Lalbagh resident Faria Ahmed Borsha said gas sometimes came at night, but the pressure was too low for cooking.
“Sometimes gas comes at night, but the pressure is too low to cook,” she said.
To cope with the shortage, her family spent around Tk4,000 on an electric stove, which has pushed up their electricity bill.
“Previously, our monthly electricity bill was around Tk2,000. Since we started using the electric stove, it has averaged around Tk4,000,” Faria said.
For their prepaid electricity connection, the family had already spent Tk2,500 between September 1 and September 17.
“It is not only about the money. Food cooked on an electric stove does not taste the same, and it is not comfortable for cooking,” she said.
Her husband, Md Robin, said their household expenses had increased significantly because of the gas crisis.
“Our salary does not increase every month, but because of the gas crisis, we have to spend an extra Tk2,000 to Tk3,000 every month,” he said.
He said that around four months ago, they could occasionally get some gas in the evening, particularly on Fridays, but even that had become unreliable.
Another Lalbagh resident, housewife Fahmida Yasmin, said her family had faced the same problem for several months.
“Since Eid-ul-Azha, we do not even know when the gas comes and when it goes. For months, we have hardly been able to cook with gas,” she said.
As a result, the family has been using an electric stove, adding around Tk1,500 to Tk2,000 to its monthly expenses.
Residents said families with young children face additional difficulties, as they struggle to heat water, warm food and prepare milk without a functioning gas supply.
The problem is also affecting tenants in other parts of the capital.
Kamal Pasha, who lives in a rented house on Zakir Hossain Road in Mohammadpur, said the situation had become so difficult that he had even considered leaving.
His family gets up before dawn to cook when gas is available. At other times, they have to use an electric stove.
Although he cannot regularly cook on the gas stove, he still pays Tk1,080 every month to his landlord as a gas charge along with the rent.
In some areas, residents said gas pressure remains almost nonexistent during the day, forcing families to wait until late at night to cook.
For bachelor and private-sector employee Tapu Chandra Das, who lives in Shewrapara, the crisis has changed his entire cooking routine.
“Proper gas supply has been unavailable for several months. Sometimes I have to buy food from hotels,” he said.
He said gas sometimes becomes available after 2am and remains available until around 5am.
“On days when I have office in the morning, I stay awake at night and cook enough food for five or six days. Then I only have to buy rice from hotels,” he said.
But even that option has become more expensive.
Tapu said hotels previously sold rice separately, but many now require customers to buy curry as well.
“After the gas crisis began, some hotels also increased the prices of curries. A curry that used to cost Tk20 now costs Tk30, while one that cost Tk40 is now Tk60,” he said.
In some cases, he added, prices have remained unchanged but the quantity has been reduced.
For bachelor Shimul Hossain in Mirpur 11, the crisis has also affected access to drinking water.
“Because of the gas crisis, we are facing a serious problem with drinking water. Sometimes we have to buy water from outside. Previously, we used to boil water before drinking, but now we cannot do that because of the lack of gas,” he said.
He said he and his friends now use a rice cooker to heat drinking water, although that is not always convenient.
Some households said frequent load-shedding was also making electric stoves unreliable. In several cases, electricity goes out after cooking has begun, forcing families to wait for power to return.
Others have resorted to LPG stoves or traditional clay stoves.
The household crisis comes amid a wider national gas shortage.
According to Petrobangla figures cited by relevant sources, daily gas demand is around 380 crore cubic feet, while supply has generally been managed at around 265-270 crore cubic feet. LNG contributes around 99-105 crore cubic feet, while domestic gas fields provide about 162 crore cubic feet.
The shortage worsened after a fire on July 21 damaged electrical systems at US-based Excelerate Energy’s floating LNG terminal in Moheshkhali, disrupting around 450 million cubic feet per day of supply. Contemporary reports at the time also said the disruption reduced national grid supply by around 450 million cubic feet per day.
Partial supply later resumed, but the disruption contributed to shortages affecting households, industries and power generation.
The crisis has continued to affect consumers, with Titas warning that severely low gas pressure would persist across its distribution network until the LNG supply situation improved.
Experts say there is no immediate solution to the country's gas crisis, but increasing domestic gas production could help.
The shortage is also hurting gas-dependent industries, including textile, knitwear, dyeing and finishing factories. Some have had to suspend production, while others are operating below capacity.
Advocate SM Nazer Hossain, vice-president of the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB), told Dhaka Tribune that consumers should not be expected to pay the full bill when the promised service is not being provided.
“The government has committed to providing uninterrupted gas connections. But you are not providing that service. Then why should you collect the full bill?” he said.
He said the additional costs were particularly burdensome for salaried people, whose incomes generally do not increase regularly.
“There should be a specific plan from the government to deal with the fuel crisis. But we do not see any such specific plan from the government. We have never seen one,” he said.
He alleged that the government often resorts to unplanned price increases whenever a crisis emerges instead of addressing the underlying problems.
“We have seen this before when fuel prices were increased. The government raises prices whenever there is a crisis, but fails to resolve the crisis in a proper and planned manner,” Nazer said.
Asked about households that have been paying gas bills for months despite receiving little or no gas, Titas Gas Managing Director Shahnewaz Parvez told Dhaka Tribune that the company had no scope to waive or reduce bills because of existing billing policies.
“Despite Titas’s willingness to help consumers in various ways, we do not have the authority to waive or reduce gas bills because of the existing policies governing gas billing,” he said.
He said installing prepaid gas meters for all consumers could prevent such problems in the future.
“Installing prepaid meters is very important. If prepaid meters are installed for all consumers, this problem will no longer persist,” Parvez said.
Although Titas began installing prepaid gas meters several years ago, the program has yet to be fully implemented across its customer base.
Explaining the ongoing gas shortage in residential areas, Parvez said reduced gas production and supply had resulted in lower allocations for Titas, making it difficult to ensure adequate supply to households.
He also said the industrial and power sectors were given priority in gas distribution, with residential consumers receiving supply afterward.
“Gas is supplied first to industrial areas and the power sector. Residential consumers come afterward,” Parvez said.
He added that the shortage in residential areas could not be resolved unless the overall gas supply increased.

item.title: A year after Liza’s death, DU halls still lack uniform emergency care
item.description:
During the exam period, at around 1am, a residential student of Dhaka University’s Shamsun Nahar Hall suddenly fell seriously ill in her room.
Her roommates became concerned after learning about her condition. Later, with the help of two hall employees, she was taken by ambulance to Dhaka Medical College Hospital.
After receiving treatment, the student returned to the hall the following day. According to her, she was not allowed to stay in the hall after returning and was advised to sit for her exams from the home of a local guardian.
The incident raises questions about how sick students in residential halls are provided medical care during emergencies at night, whether basic treatment and emergency equipment are available in the halls, and how prepared the university is before a student reaches the central medical centre.
Shaheed Buddhijibi Dr Mohammad Mortoza Medical Centre at Dhaka University. Photo: Collected
Similar questions were raised after the death of Asma Akter Liza, a student of Bangamata Sheikh Fazilatunnesa Mujib Hall, in August 2025.
Liza died in hospital on August 15 after falling ill. Following her death, students alleged that there were shortages of emergency medical equipment, stretchers and immediate medical support in the hall.
The university administration subsequently promised to improve its healthcare services. It also said a fact-finding committee had been formed to investigate allegations of negligence against doctors at the medical centre and that steps had been taken to recruit new doctors.
But a year later, questions remain about how far those initiatives have reached the residential halls.
There have been changes in the university’s central healthcare system since Liza’s death.
On August 20, 2025, the University of Dhaka and the Turkish Cooperation and Coordination Agency (TİKA) signed a memorandum of understanding. Under the agreement, the medical centre was to be renovated and equipped with modern medical equipment, along with the provision of a modern ambulance.
The renovated medical centre was inaugurated on February 18, 2026, with support from TİKA. The project included an X-ray machine, ECG, analyser, microscope, hospital beds and other equipment.
According to current university information, the medical centre provides healthcare services 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with 30 doctors working in different shifts. It also has dental, eye and X-ray units, isolation facilities and a small operation theatre.
However, improvements to the central medical centre do not necessarily address emergency response capacity inside the residential halls.
When a student falls seriously ill at 1am, the first few minutes can determine how quickly she receives medical attention. Who will assist her? How will she be taken out of the hall? Where is a stretcher or wheelchair available? How long will it take for an ambulance to arrive?
At Shamsun Nahar Hall, a sick room, some emergency medicines and a wheelchair have currently been arranged through an initiative of the hall parliament, according to hall parliament members.
They also said that in cases of serious illness at night, students are taken to hospital with the help of the provost and floor teachers.
Ruqayyah Hall resident student Nazifa Tasnim said: “We have first-aid supplies in our hall, but there is no sickroom. I have never heard of a sickroom in our hall. As far as I know, Sufia Kamal Hall has a sickroom.”
The situation, however, is not the same in all halls.
Ashura Khatun, a resident student of Bangamata Sheikh Fazilatunnesa Mujib Hall, said: “We do not have a sick room or a sick boy (a designated contact in case of health emergencies) in our hall. Although there is a doctor, the doctor does not have enough medical equipment.”
According to her, when someone falls ill at night, the floor teacher is informed first and an ambulance is arranged if necessary. However, she claimed that floor teachers do not always answer their phones.
Abrar Harun, a student of Muktijoddha Ziaur Rahman Hall, said: “I know about the sick boy. He can be reached by phone when needed. But there is no sick room in the hall. In emergencies, sick students are taken to Dhaka Medical College Hospital or Mortaza Medical Centre.”
Sabbirul Islam, a student of Sergeant Zahurul Haq Hall, said: “There is no sick room in our hall. If a student suddenly falls ill, they are generally taken to Mortaza Medical Centre or Dhaka Medical College Hospital.”
He also said that although he knew there was a “sick boy” in the hall, he did not know the person’s name, identity or phone number.
Similar arrangements are also reported to be in place at Bijoy Ekattor Hall, Kabi Jasimuddin Hall, Surya Sen Hall, Mohsin Hall and Bangabandhu Hall. In these halls, sick boys provide necessary assistance to ill students, but there are no separate sick rooms.
Residential halls have health workers, commonly known as “sick boys”, to assist students when they fall ill. Depending on the hall, one or more health workers are assigned to the role.
Their duties include checking on sick students and delivering necessary food, drinks and medicine to their rooms.
However, it is not clear whether they are trained in emergency medical care or whether they know CPR or basic first aid.
Dr Meherin Parsh, assistant medical officer, said: “The main responsibility of sick boys or hall staff is not to provide medical treatment. However, they need training on how to safely move a patient during an emergency and when to take the patient to a doctor.”
When a student becomes seriously ill at 1am, there should be a specific emergency pathway at educational institutions. From providing initial assistance in the room and contacting the responsible person to arranging a stretcher or wheelchair, calling an ambulance, reaching the medical centre, getting necessary medicine and referring the student to a hospital if needed, protocol should dictate who is responsible at each stage.
But under the current system, the process varies from hall to hall.
Some halls have sick rooms, while others do not. Some have wheelchairs, while students in other halls do not even know where such equipment is available. In some halls, health workers can be reached by phone, while in others, students do not know their identity or phone numbers.
In emergency healthcare, the number of ambulances is important, but response time is also crucial.
The university’s current instructions provide 01798762920 as the emergency and ambulance number. The same instructions say students can access ambulances and call services through a call slip from the hall authorities. How long this process takes during an emergency at night is an important question.
On this issue, Meherin Parsh said: “Emergency patients are given priority when requesting an ambulance. We try to send an ambulance as quickly as possible after receiving a call.”
According to university information, emergency medical services are available 24 hours a day, but the medical centre’s pharmacy remains open from 8am to 8pm.
The health card and token section is also open from 8:15am to 8pm.
This means that even if a student receives medical advice after 8pm, she does not have access to medicines from the regular dispensary.
The pharmacy at the university’s club premises also remains open until 8pm, students said.
As a result, students have to go to pharmacies outside the residential halls to obtain medicines.
After Liza’s death, questions were also raised about emergency healthcare and students’ ability to leave the women’s halls at night.
Currently, the instructions of Kabi Sufia Kamal Hall ask sick students to contact the hall’s medical team, the staff on duty at the gate or the relevant floor teacher.
But if a seriously ill female student needs to be taken to hospital at midnight, it is not clear whether there is a hall-specific protocol stating exactly who will open the gate, whose permission will be required and what the alternative arrangement will be if the person responsible does not answer the phone.
A residential teacher at Kabi Sufia Kamal Hall, speaking on condition of anonymity, said: “There is no question of denying any student medical care during an emergency. If necessary, the student is taken to hospital in coordination with the responsible teacher, hall authorities and the student’s guardian.”
Assistant Proctor of Dhaka University Sharmin Kabir said: “The university has taken several steps to improve healthcare services. The medical centre has been modernised, and new equipment and ambulances have been added. The administration is also considering better coordination of emergency services at the hall level.”
A year after Liza’s death, the university’s central medical centre has undergone significant infrastructural changes, including renovation and the addition of medical equipment and an ambulance.
But emergency healthcare arrangements inside the residential halls remain uneven. Some halls have sick rooms and wheelchairs, while others do not have separate sick rooms. There are also differences in the availability of health workers, emergency equipment and access to responsible personnel.
At the same time, university information says emergency services are available 24 hours a day, while the medical centre’s dispensary remains open until 8pm. The university has also said that female doctors are available on call for female students at night.
For students living in the halls, however, the critical question remains what happens between the moment an emergency occurs in a room and the moment the student reaches professional medical care.
